(a) 
After the date of enactment of this Act, promotion-list officers shall be promoted to and appointed in the permanent grade of brigadier general in the Regular Army only as hereinafter in this section prescribed, except in those cases governed by the provisions of section 513 of this title, and except in those cases governed by the proviso to the first sentence of subsection 507 (d) of this title.

 
    (b) 
Based upon the number of vacancies existing and anticipated in the grade of brigadier general in the Regular Army and the number of officers desired in that grade, the Secretary of War shall direct a selection board to select and recommend a prescribed number of officers for promotion to that grade, and, in order to insure that the Army will have adequate numbers of officers in the grade of brigadier general with experience qualifying them for service in or with the several branches, arms, and services, he may, in his discretion, direct that, of the number to be selected and recommended, specified numbers have experience qualifying them for service in or with certain specified branches, arms or services. The Secretary of War shall furnish to such board a list of the names of the officers to be considered. The list of names furnished for consideration shall include the names of the senior officers below the junior in the permanent grade of brigadier general whose names are not carried on the recommended list for promotion to the grade of brigadier general and the names of additional such officers in the order that their names appear next below theirs on the applicable promotion lists, as the Secretary of War may prescribe, and, until June 30, 1948, in addition thereto may include the names of any officers in permanent grade below that of brigadier general who served during the current war in any general officer grade under temporary appointment. From among the officers named for consideration, the designated selection board shall select and recommend the prescribed number, including any prescribed numbers whose experience qualifies them for service m or with a designated branch, arm, or service. The officers selected and recommended shall be those who, in the opinion of the board, are the best qualified officers of those listed for consideration.
 
    (c) 
The names of officers who are selected and recommended for promotion to the grade of brigadier general in the Regular Army shall be carried on a permanent recommended list of officers for promotion to that grade. Upon selection, the names of such officers shall be placed on the recommended list at the foot thereof arranged among themselves according to precedence to be determined by the Secretary of War. The number of officers to be selected and recommended by designated selection boards for promotion to the grade of brigadier general in the Regular Army shall be determined by the Secretary of War. It is not mandatory that the Secretary of War direct the selection and recommendation of numbers sufficient to produce the number authorized for that grade; but officers who are selected and recommended for promotion to that grade by any such selection board, and whose names are not removed from the recommended list by the President, shall be nominated, and by and with the advice and consent of the Senate appointed, in that grade as soon as there is a vacancy in the number authorized for that grade.
 
    (d) 
The ratio of the number of officers which the Secretary of War names for consideration by any selection board for promotion to the grade of brigadier general in the Regular Army, to the number of officers which he directs such selection board to select from among those so named, may be as desired by the. Secretary of War, but no officer shall be considered or selected by any selection board more than one year prior to the date on which it is anticipated he will, if selected, be appointed in that grade. After June 30, 1949, officers must have completed at least one year’s service under permanent appointment in the grade of colonel in the Regular Army, before being nominated or appointed in the grade of brigadier general in the Regular Army.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that a "selection board" making recommendations, plus Senate advice and consent, amounts to an advisory body taking part in a federal decision. But the selection board is an internal Army body convened by the Secretary of War to rank officers for promotion, and the President and Senate are likewise inside the federal government. No state, tribe, company, outside expert, or member of the public is consulted, and no rulemaking, hearing, or right to sue is created.
fable.s: the Secretary of War shall direct a selection board to select and recommend a prescribed number of officers for promotion to that grade

qwen_block.w: This section describes an internal military promotion process where a selection board, directed by the Secretary of War, selects officers for promotion. All actors involved (the Secretary of War, the selection board, and the officers being considered) are part of the federal government (specifically the military). There is no consultation with or participation by entities outside the federal government, such as the public, states, or non-federal experts.
qwen_block.s: the Secretary of War shall direct a selection board to select and recommend a prescribed number of officers for promotion to that grade... The Secretary of War shall furnish to such board a list of the names of the officers to be considered.
qwen_block.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the "selection board" constitutes an advisory body involving outside experts or public participation. However, the text specifies that the Secretary of War furnishes the list of officers to be considered and that the board selects from among those officers. These are internal military personnel matters. The board is composed of military officers (implied by the context of selecting officers for promotion within the Regular Army), and the process is entirely within the executive branch's military hierarchy. There is no mention of state governments, the general public, non-federal experts, or other outside entities participating in the decision. Therefore, it is intra-governmental coordination/decision-making, not participation.

opus.w: The section sets out how Army officers are promoted to brigadier general. It does this through military selection boards, the Secretary of War, the President, and Senate confirmation, all of which are inside the federal government. There is no public comment, hearing, outside advisory body, consultation with states or tribes, or right to sue. The board and the 'advice and consent' language look procedural, but they never cross the federal boundary, so this is not participation.
opus.s: the Secretary of War shall direct a selection board to select and recommend a prescribed number of officers for promotion to that grade
opus.b: The tempting reading is that the "selection board" and the Senate's "advice and consent" are forms of participation. Neither is. Army promotion selection boards are made up of serving officers, who are inside the federal government. The Senate is part of Congress, which is also inside the federal government. No one outside the federal government takes part in any decision here.

qwen_chat.w: The section describes an internal military promotion process where a selection board, directed by the Secretary of War, recommends officers for promotion. All actors involved (Secretary of War, selection board, officers) are part of the federal government/military. There is no consultation or coordination with entities outside the federal government, such as states, tribes, the public, or private organizations. Therefore, it does not meet the definition of participation.
qwen_chat.s: the Secretary of War shall direct a selection board to select and recommend a prescribed number of officers for promotion to that grade
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the "selection board" constitutes an advisory body involving outside experts or stakeholders participating in the promotion decision. However, the text specifies that the board is directed by the Secretary of War and selects from a list of officers provided by the Secretary. These are internal military personnel and processes. There is no mention of state governments, the general public, private companies, or independent experts being involved in the selection or recommendation process. The entire mechanism is internal to the Department of War (now Defense) and the military chain of command.
